name: Binga Bank (Binga State Bank)
description: Chicago's first Black-owned bank: founded as a private bank by Jesse Binga in 1908 (drawing $200,000+ in deposits on opening day) and chartered as the Binga State Bank in 1921 — the first Black-owned state-chartered bank in Chicago. Headquartered at 35th & South State Streets with the five-story Arcade Building (1929), it served a community shut out of white-owned banks. The bank closed in 1930 in the Great Depression; Binga was convicted of embezzlement in 1933, served three years, and died in Chicago in 1950.

name: Binga State Bank
description: Jesse Binga's pioneering Black-owned Chicago bank

name: Community Bank of Lawndale / Covenant Bank
description: First Black-owned bank on Chicago's West Side (1977), founded by Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall; bought in 2008 by Living Word Christian Center with investments from 3,000+ church members and renamed Covenant Bank; closed by regulators 2013.

name: Covenant Bank
description: Faith-capitalized Black community bank on Chicago's West Side (2008-2013); bought from Community Bank of Lawndale by Rev. Bill Winston, funded by thousands of small church-linked shareholders, closed by regulators with deposits assumed by Liberty Bank and Trust.

name: Douglass National Bank
description: Douglass National Bank was a Black-owned bank founded by Anthony Overton and named for Frederick Douglass, operating from the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619–3627 S. State Street in Bronzeville. A Library of Congress research guide, citing Robert E. Weems Jr.'s The Merchant Prince of Black Chicago (2020), identifies it as the second nationally chartered Black-owned bank in the United States; CTL's banking brief flags that an NPS-derived source in the same corpus calls it the first, and this record carries the contradiction openly rather than resolving it by preference. The Kansas City Fed dates its opening to 1922 (other sources give 1921 or 1923 — disputed), and its national bank charter was number 12227. Its officers included President Anthony Overton and Cashier Arthur J. Wilson. After Binga State Bank closed in 1930, Douglass was the only surviving Black bank in Chicago; it failed in 1932 during the Great Depression. Tier is R: the founding year and the first/second ranking are both disputed in CTL's own evidence, and the graph record rests on a single secondary source.

name: Highland Community Bank
description: Black-owned community bank on Chicago's South Side (1970-2015); closed January 23, 2015 by Illinois regulators for operating in an unsafe and unsound condition with inadequate capital; all deposits assumed by United Fidelity Bank of Evansville, Indiana.

name: Illinois Service Federal Savings & Loan Association
description: Black-owned Chicago thrift founded 1934 when 13 Black South Side leaders pooled $7,000 to make mortgages where white-owned banks would not lend; founders included property manager (later CHA chairman) Robert Taylor and insurance executive A.W. Williams (35 years, president and board chairman). Main office at 4619 S. Martin Luther King Drive, Bronzeville. Demutualized and recapitalized by Ghana's Groupe Nduom in 2016, renamed GN Bank in 2018. NOTE: this record duplicates CTL-E-1251 ('Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan / ISF Bank / GN Bank'); both are retained per the append-only rule pending a coordinator merge decision.
aliases: Illinois Service Federal; ISF Bank; Illinois Federal Savings and Loan; GN Bank (Chicago)

name: Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan / ISF Bank / GN Bank
description: Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan — founded 1934 by 13 Black men during the Great Migration — was Chicago's historic Black-owned thrift at 4619 S. Martin Luther King Drive in Bronzeville. Acquired by Groupe Nduom in April 2016 after a voluntary supervisory conversion, it was rebranded GN Bank in July 2018, remaining African-American-owned.
aliases: GN Bank; ISF Bank; Illinois Service Federal

name: Independence Bank of Chicago
description: Black-owned bank founded 1964 to serve the Chatham-Avalon community
neighborhood: 79th Street commercial corridor (Chatham / Greater Grand Crossing); Chatham

name: Seaway National Bank
description: Black-owned South Side bank serving Chatham and the South Side
neighborhood: 87th Street commercial development (Chatham / Auburn Gresham); Chatham

name: Washington Park National Bank
description: Historic South Side bank whose 1924 Neoclassical headquarters at 63rd & Cottage Grove (Albert A. Schwartz, architect) is the Washington Park National Bank Building; the bank closed June 8, 1931.
status_today: standing (vacant, threatened as of 2019-2020; 2026 status unresolved)

name: All Nations Pentecostal Church
description: Bronzeville Pentecostal congregation founded by a formerly enslaved-generation Georgia migrant woman; healing ministry, interracial membership, radio pioneer, Depression-era feeding program.

name: Apostolic Church of God
description: Large South Side Oneness Pentecostal congregation at 6320 S. Dorchester Ave., Woodlawn. Rev. Arthur M. Brazier merged his Universal Church of Christ congregation with ACOG in 1960 and pastored it until June 1, 2008 (succeeded by his son Dr. Byron T. Brazier); campus milestones include the 1977 sanctuary at 63rd & Kenwood and the 1992 campus at 63rd & Dorchester.

name: Beautiful Zion Missionary Baptist Church
description: Beautiful Zion Missionary Baptist Church, 1406 W. 64th St. (Englewood, Chicago); received a $10,000 Timuel D. Black, Jr. Grant Fund award (Feb 2025) for masonry repairs to its Neoclassical limestone façade; a community cornerstone for more than a century.

name: Bethel AME Church
description: African Methodist Episcopal congregation at 4440 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago (Grand Boulevard/Bronzeville). Organized in June 1862 as a mission church of Quinn Chapel by Bishop William Paul Quinn after Quinn Chapel's overcrowding; occupied 17 locations before settling at its current site in 1949; celebrated its 155th anniversary June 24–25, 2017, under pastor Rev. Jennifer Tinsley, with Bishop Anne Henning Byfield (16th Episcopal District) as anniversary preacher. Member congregation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (CTL-E-1492).

name: Blackwell-Israel Samuel A.M.E. Zion Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 3956 S. Langley Ave. is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1886).

name: Canaan Baptist Church of Christ
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 6657-59 S Harvard Av is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1904-05).

name: Christian Tabernacle Church
description: Christian Tabernacle Church is a Chicago congregation founded by the Rev. Maceo Woods at 47th Street and Prairie Avenue in the Grand Boulevard neighborhood; the church's own site gives its address as 4712 S. Prairie Ave. Woods founded the church in 1959, after serving as music minister at Hyde Park Bible Church, and the congregation grew from a founding handful to more than 800 members within its first year; its 60th anniversary was marked in 2019. Its choir — the Christian Tabernacle Concert Choir — became one of Chicago gospel's signature recording ensembles, releasing albums with Woods for Vee-Jay, Volt/Stax's Gospel Truth line, Savoy, and Arista across five decades, including Hello Sunshine (1970), recorded live at the church. In the early 1960s the church's gospel programming brought Detroit's Rev. C. L. Franklin to Chicago, with his daughter Aretha Franklin singing. Woods pastored the church until his death on January 11, 2020; the congregation continues at the Prairie Avenue address.
aliases: Christian Tabernacle Church of Chicago; Christian Tabernacle Baptist Church

name: Corpus Christi Catholic Church
description: Historic Black Catholic parish in Bronzeville

name: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer
description: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer is a South Side Chicago congregation founded on April 29, 1959, by gospel singer and pastor Dr. Charles G. Hayes, beginning in the basement of a home at 634 Woodland Park. Gospel historian Robert M. Marovich counts it among the first Chicago churches to adopt the new Detroit gospel choral style. The congregation grew through a Cottage Grove Avenue storefront and, from 1961, a converted post office on South Langley Avenue, before settling at 842 East 65th Street in Woodlawn, the corner of 65th and Maryland the church calls "Love Corner." Its choir, the Warriors, became one of the most successful recording and radio church choirs in gospel history, releasing more than thirty albums and carrying Hayes's Sunday-night broadcasts; signature recordings include "Jesus Can Work It Out" and "Step Back, Let God Do It."
aliases: Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer of Chicago; Cosmo

name: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church
description: Historic Bronzeville Missionary Baptist congregation

name: Evangelical Bethel Church of Chicago
description: Haitian congregation in Chicago's Rogers Park neighborhood, sharing the Rogers Park Baptist Church building at 1900 W. Greenleaf Avenue. Documented by the Rogers Park/West Ridge Historical Society among Rogers Park churches; the building is also shared by the Spanish congregation Cristo En La Ciudad.

name: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church
description: South Side Baptist church founded by Rev. Clay Evans

name: First Baptist Congregational Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 60 N Ashland Av is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1869-71).

name: First Church of Deliverance
description: Metropolitan Spiritual Churches of Christ congregation at 4315 S. Wabash Ave., Chicago (Bronzeville). Founded 1929 by Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs; pioneer of Black religious radio (1935) and television (1953); famed 200-member choir and gospel recordings; at its peak among the largest Black congregations in Chicago.

name: First Presbyterian Church of Chicago
description: First Presbyterian Church of Chicago at 6400 S. Kimbark Ave., Woodlawn. Founded June 26, 1833 — the oldest continuously operating institution in Chicago. Current Gothic Revival building (Thomas Tallmadge & Vernon S. Watson) built 1927; the first public school and first Head Start programs in the region started in its buildings; hosted the Shrine of Christ the King congregation after the October 2015 fire.

name: Greater Harvest Missionary Baptist Church
description: South Side church associated with the Roberta Martin gospel tradition
aliases: Greater Harvest; Greater Harvest Baptist Church

name: Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church
description: Baptist congregation at 6035 Princeton Street, Englewood (presently Mount Hope Baptist Church). Under pastor Rev. William Lambert — a 1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, Georgia, and a Clergy Alliance of Chicago leader in the selective-buying campaign — the church supported the development of Operation Breadbasket and in August 1966 became the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement.

name: Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church / Chicago Freedom Movement South Side Action Center
description: Baptist church at 6035 S. Princeton St., Englewood. In August 1966 it became the South Side Action Center of the Chicago Freedom Movement under pastor Rev. William Lambert (1962 Chicago delegate to Albany, GA; Clergy Alliance selective-buying campaign leader). NOTE: possible duplicate of CTL-E-1391 ("Greater Mount Hope Baptist Church") — merged 2026-10-05 per founder review.

name: Greater Saint John AME Church
description: Active African Methodist Episcopal congregation at 6201 S Throop St, Chicago IL 60636 (West Englewood), pastored by Georgetta Glover. Runs a food-bank ministry; Sunday worship 10:30 AM-1:00 PM. Member congregation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (CTL-E-1492). Distinct from Greater St. John Bible Church (1256 N Waller).
aliases: Greater St. John AME Church; Greater St John AME Church

name: Greater Salem Baptist Church
description: Chicago Baptist congregation; Mahalia Jackson's first Chicago church home after her 1927 arrival, and the base of her early choir work and the Johnson Brothers/Johnson Gospel Singers. Within months of arriving, Jackson was the lead vocalist of the 50-member choir and joined the pastor's sons (Prince, Wilbur, and Robert Johnson) and Louise Lemon in the Johnson Singers — described as Chicago's first Black gospel group. The Johnson Brothers were the first organized group to play the Chicago church circuit, staging self-written musical dramas at the church with Jackson in the lead role before splitting in the mid-1930s. The congregation continues today as Greater Salem Missionary Baptist Church on Chicago's South Side.

name: Greater Tabernacle Cathedral
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 11300-12 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1890).

name: Greater Union Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 1956 W. Warren Boulevard is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1886).

name: Holy Angels Catholic Church
description: Bronzeville Catholic parish at 607 E. Oakwood Blvd.; Clements was its first Black pastor (1969-1991); now the main worship site of Our Lady of Africa Parish.

name: Holy Name Cathedral
description: Tallest-building lists of the era excluded churches and cathedrals

name: Kingdom Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 301 N. Central is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1926-1943).
aliases: Fifteenth Church of Christ, Scientist; 15th Church of Christ, Scientist

name: Liberty Baptist Church
description: Bronzeville Baptist church founded 1919; its pastor Rev. A.P. Jackson hosted Dr. King during the Chicago Freedom Movement

name: Life Center COGIC
description: Life Center COGIC — the Life Center Church of God in Christ, known to its congregation as the Prayer Palace — is a Pentecostal congregation at 5500 South Indiana Avenue in Chicago's Washington Park neighborhood, led for nearly five decades by Pastor T. L. Barrett. Barrett began pastoring in 1966 and led Mt. Zion Baptist Church, at 5512 South Indiana Avenue, from the late 1960s; after a theological disagreement with that church's elders, he left in 1976 to form his own ministry, the Life Center COGIC church, in the same neighborhood. The congregation is the institutional home of Barrett's youth-focused ministry, the work carried on the records of Pastor T.L. Barrett and the Youth for Christ Choir, whose 1970s gospel recordings later drew a national audience. Barrett's congregation remained with him through the court-ordered restitution of the 1990s, which he completed, and in April 2024 the church community marked his stepping back from the pulpit with a three-day celebration honoring Barrett and his wife, Cleopatra Barrett, including a gospel concert at Life Center COGIC.
aliases: Life Center Church of God in Christ; The Life Center C.O.G.I.C.; Life Center Church of Universal Awareness; The Prayer Palace

name: Living Word Christian Center
description: Living Word Christian Center is a nondenominational Word of Faith congregation in Forest Park, Illinois, founded by Dr. Bill Winston and his wife, Dr. Veronica Winston. The ministry began in 1988 with weekend Faith Crusades run from Minneapolis; the Winstons moved to Chicago that December and opened a Bible training school at the Quality Inn at Madison and Halsted, becoming the Living Word Church of Chicago in 1989 and Living Word Christian Center in 1990. After meeting at Forest Park's Chez Roué Banquet Hall from 1994 to 1997, the church bought the declining 33-acre Forest Park Mall and held its first service there on New Year's Eve 1997. Its worship center at 7600 West Roosevelt Road, built from the mall and its movie complex, anchors a campus that includes the Joseph Business School and the redeveloped Forest Park Plaza.
aliases: LWCC; Living Word Church of Chicago

name: Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church
description: Apostolic congregation at 4100 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, Chicago (Grand Boulevard), in a Richardsonian Romanesque building (1890; 1913) designated a Chicago Landmark in 2007. Descends from the interracial, nonsectarian Metropolitan Community Church (1920), which hosted Ida B. Wells-Barnett, Robert S. Abbott, Gwendolyn Brooks, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, and Eleanor Roosevelt. Led for 20 years by senior pastor Rev. Dr. Leon D. Finney Jr. (d. 2020), Woodlawn organizer and developer.
aliases: Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church Building; The Met

name: Metropolitan Missionary Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 2151 W Washington Blvd is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1901).

name: Monumental Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 729 E. Oakwood Boulevard is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1899-1901).

name: Morning Star Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 3993 S. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Drive is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1921).

name: Mt. Pisgah Missionary Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 4600-4628 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1912).

name: Mt. Zion Baptist Church
description: Mt. Zion Baptist Church was a Washington Park, Chicago congregation pastored from 1968 to 1976 by the Rev. T. L. Barrett — the pastorate in which Barrett formed his Youth for Christ Choir and began the recording career collected decades later in the box set I Shall Wear a Crown. Barrett, whose pulpit career began in 1966, took the Mt. Zion pulpit in 1968; there he built a youth-focused ministry whose roughly forty-voice teenage choir recorded Like a Ship (Without a Sail) in 1971. In 1976, after a theological disagreement with the church's elders, Barrett left to found the Life Center Church of God in Christ in the same neighborhood. Sources conflict on the congregation's own frame: a 1998 Congressional tribute says Barrett organized Mt. Zion in 1968 and carried it to a new location in 1983, where it was renamed Life Center; biographical accounts describe an existing church he joined in 1968 and left in 1976. The congregation's institutional history outside Barrett's pastorate is unresolved in the sources consulted; this record stages the documented Barrett-era congregation, not a full institutional history.
aliases: Mount Zion Baptist Church (Washington Park, Chicago)

name: New Covenant Missionary Baptist Church
description: South Side Chicago Baptist congregation at 740 E. 77th Street; founded by Elijah Thurston; pastored by three generations of the Thurston family.

name: New Friendship Baptist Church
description: Baptist church at 854 W. 71st Street, Englewood, pastored by Rev. Stroy Freeman. First major staging area for Chicago Freedom Movement rallies and marches on the South Side (1966): Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'My place is in Gage Park' speech (August 4, 1966, with Mahalia Jackson) and the July 29, 1966 march to Halverson Realty both launched from the church.

name: New Genesis Assembly of God Baptist Church
description: Black Baptist congregation at 1400 N. Laramie Avenue, Austin, in an eclectic Neo-Gothic building (1924–1949) designated a Chicago Landmark in 2025. Built as the Trinity Evangelical Lutheran Church (congregation est. 1870; architect Moritz F. Strauch); became home to the New Genesis Assembly of God Baptist Church in 1997 after the neighborhood's racial transition.

name: New Life Covenant Church Southeast
description: New Life Covenant Church Southeast is a nondenominational, multicultural congregation on Chicago's South Side founded and led by Pastor John F. Hannah. Church accounts describe a start on January 27, 2010, with about sixty people at a Wednesday-night Bible study. The congregation became known for an intense prayer culture — 4 AM prayer gatherings, twelve-hour prayer events, and the annual Prayer on the 9 march that lines 79th Street — and worshiped at a site it calls The Tabernacle, at 78th and Dobson. In September 2021 it opened The Temple, a 100,000-square-foot, 4,000-seat worship and performing-arts facility at 7621 South Greenwood Avenue in Greater Grand Crossing, a project Hannah framed as economic redevelopment of an underserved African American community. The record is distinct from the separate, older New Life Covenant Church in Humboldt Park.
aliases: New Life Covenant Southeast; NLCSE; NLC Southeast

name: Olivet Baptist Church
description: Historic Bronzeville Baptist church, among the largest Black congregations of its era

name: Original Providence Baptist Church
description: Historic Black Baptist congregation at 515 N. Pine Avenue, Austin — founded 1866 by former slaves, Chicago's third-oldest Black church. Building constructed 1902 by the First Baptist Church of Austin (architects Brown, Burton & Davis; Gothic/Tudor Revival), with an attached 1928 school; designated a Chicago Landmark in 2026.

name: Our Lady of Africa Parish
description: Bronzeville parish formed July 1, 2021 from five merged parishes; Holy Angels is its main worship site.

name: Pilgrim Baptist Church
description: Bronzeville church known as the birthplace of gospel music under Thomas A. Dorsey

name: Quinn Chapel AME Church
description: Chicago's first African American church congregation, rooted in Bronzeville

name: Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ
description: Church at 4021 S. State St; site of Emmett Till's open-casket visitation and funeral in September 1955.

name: Rogers Park Baptist Church
description: Baptist congregation at 1900 W. Greenleaf Avenue, Rogers Park, Chicago; founded October 22, 1891; host congregation whose building is shared by Evangelical Bethel Church of Chicago (Haitian) and Cristo En La Ciudad (Spanish).

name: Saint Michael's Church
description: St. Michael's, Old Town

name: Salem Baptist Church of Chicago
description: Baptist megachurch at 752 E 114th Street in Chicago's Pullman community area; founded 1985 by Rev. James T. Meeks; dedicated the 10,000-seat House of Hope auditorium in 2005; senior pastor Rev. Dr. Charlie E. Dates since January 8, 2023.

name: Shrine of Christ the King
description: Roman Catholic shrine at 6401 S. Woodlawn Ave., Woodlawn, now administered by the Institute of Christ the King Sovereign Priest. Founded as St. Clara parish (1894); Renaissance Revival church by Henry J. Schlacks finished 1928; renamed St. Clara–St. Cyril (1969) and St. Gelasius (1990); closed 2002; designated a Chicago Landmark January 14, 2004; damaged by fires in 1976 and 2015.
aliases: Shrine of Christ the King Sovereign Priest; St. Clara; St. Clara–St. Cyril; St. Gelasius

name: St. Ambrose Parish
description: Chicago Catholic parish on 47th Street where George Clements was associate pastor, 1957-1962.

name: St. Benedict the African Parish (Roman Catholic)
description: Roman Catholic parish at 340 W. 66th St., Englewood, formed from the merger of eight parishes as the neighborhood became predominantly African-American; two worship sites became separate parishes in 1995 and re-merged in 2016. Distinctive African-hut-inspired architecture; included in Chicago Architecture Foundation Open House Chicago.

name: St. Dorothy Parish
description: Chicago Catholic parish on 78th Street where George Clements was associate pastor, 1962-1969.

name: St. Edmund's Episcopal Church
description: Predominantly Black Episcopal parish at 6105 S. Michigan Avenue, Chicago (Washington Park). Began 1905 as the Washington Park Mission; admitted as a parish with charter filed October 12, 1940. One of Chicago's oldest active Black Episcopalian congregations; its archives (1930-2002) are held in the CPL Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection.
aliases: Church of St. Edmund, King and Martyr; St. Edmund, King and Martyr

name: St. Mary's M.B. Church
description: St. Mary's Missionary Baptist Church is located at 1040 W.

name: St. Rita of Cascia Parish
description: Roman Catholic (Augustinian) parish at 6243 S. Fairfield Ave., Chicago Lawn, founded 1905 — described as the first Augustinian church in Chicago. United with St. Clare of Montefalco Parish effective July 1, 2020 under Renew My Church; serves a primarily Latino community. Associated St. Rita of Cascia High School (all-boys, founded 1905) remains in operation.

name: St. Sabina Catholic Church
description: St. Sabina Catholic Church is a parish of the Archdiocese of Chicago in Auburn Gresham, founded in July 1916 when Archbishop George W. Mundelein sent Rev. Thomas Egan to establish it; Egan celebrated the first Mass on July 9, 1916, in a storefront at 7915 South Ashland Avenue. Built up by Irish Catholic parishioners, it became one of Chicago's largest parishes, then nearly closed during the white-flight era. From 1981 its pastor has been Fr. Michael Pfleger — a white priest, appointed associate pastor in 1975 and, at thirty-one, the archdiocese's youngest pastor — under whom the predominantly African American parish was refocused into a national symbol of Black Catholic social-justice ministry, with a social service center, employment resource center, and senior housing serving Auburn Gresham from its campus at 1210 West 78th Place.
aliases: Saint Sabina Church; The Faith Community of Saint Sabina; St. Sabina Parish

name: Stone Temple Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 3620-3624 W. Douglas Blvd is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1926).

name: Trinity United Church of Christ
description: Prominent South Side congregation led for decades by Rev. Jeremiah Wright

name: Truevine Missionary Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 6720 S Stewart Av is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1892).

name: Victory Apostolic Church
description: Victory Apostolic Church is an Apostolic Pentecostal congregation founded by the Rev. Andrew D. Singleton Jr. Its first service was held on August 4, 1996, in Harvey, Illinois, where the young church met at a former Ramada Inn; a year later it moved to Chicago Heights, where it worshipped for twelve years and grew rapidly. In February 2009 Victory moved to its present home in Matteson, Illinois — a 12-acre campus with a 2,500-seat sanctuary, built at a reported cost of $20 million, the figures the church itself publishes. Singleton, who was mentored by Bishop Arthur M. Brazier of Chicago's Apostolic Church of God, remains senior pastor three decades on; the congregation marked its 30th anniversary in 2026. The church's published campus figures are carried here as attributed claims from its own materials, per GOV-004.
aliases: Victory Apostolic Church of Matteson; VAC Matteson

name: Warren Avenue Congregational Church
description: Warren Avenue Congregational Church at 3101 W. Warren Boulevard, East Garfield Park (the building now houses New Greater St. John Community Missionary Baptist Church). In 1966 it welcomed the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and SCLC, becoming headquarters of the Chicago Freedom Movement's West Side campaign against slum housing.
aliases: New Greater St. John Community Missionary Baptist Church (current name)

name: Alpha Suffrage Club
description: The Alpha Suffrage Club was a Chicago organization founded on January 30, 1913, by journalist and anti-lynching crusader Ida B. Wells, with white colleagues Belle Squire and Virginia Brooks. Illinois Institute of Technology's institutional history describes it as the first organization established to promote the right for Black women to vote in Illinois, formed because Black women had been largely excluded from existing local and national suffrage organizations. The club met every Wednesday evening at the Negro Fellowship League, at 3005 South State Street in Bronzeville, and set out to educate Black and working-class women on civic matters and the importance of voting as a path to electing African American candidates to public office. Wells stated its object in terms of using the vote for the advantage of Black Chicagoans, and the club sent her to Washington for the March 1913 suffrage parade, where she refused segregation and joined the Illinois contingent. The League of Women Voters of Chicago records that members built an effective political network, distributed their own newsletter, and grew to nearly two hundred members by 1916. A commemorative marker at 31st and State streets was unveiled on October 1, 2021.

name: Andy's Jazz Club
description: Chicago jazz club

name: Appomattox Club
description: Elite Black social and civic club of Chicago, organized circa 1900 in connection with Edward Wright as “black Chicago's version of the Commercial Club.” Named for the Virginia courthouse where the Civil War effectively ended, it was a political and social powerhouse where Black business and political leaders gathered to talk policy and influence elections. From 1920 it occupied a three-story stone mansion at 3632 Grand Boulevard / South Parkway (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive; building no longer stands); the address served as headquarters for the 1940 American Negro Exposition planning. Described in the Congressional Record as one of the first African American political organizations in the country. Closed in the late 1960s.

name: B.L.U.E.S.
description: Chicago blues club at 2519 N. Halsted St., opened 1979 and known by its B.L.U.E.S. marquee. It books primarily Chicago musicians — elder statesmen such as Eddie Shaw and Jimmy Johnson alongside younger club-circuit artists (Jimmy Burns, Mike Wheeler, Billy Branch, Little Ed) — in a friendly rivalry with Kingston Mines across the street. “B.L.U.E.S. keeps its offering to blues and booze.” Owner Robert Hecko, partner Bill Gilmore, manager Jennifer Littleton (per Chicago Blues Hall of Fame listings).
aliases: B.L.U.E.S. Chicago; B.L.U.E.S. on Halsted; Blues on Halsted

name: Birdland (formerly the Beige Room)
description: Jazz room in the Pershing Hotel complex at 6400 S. Cottage Grove, Woodlawn — the former Beige Room. The Pershing Hotel's Beige Room opened where El Grotto Supper Club had been (1944–1947 at 6412 S. Cottage Grove), per the Chicago Defender, Dec. 13, 1947. Arnett Cobb played the room (Defender, Dec. 24, 1955). The complex also held the Pershing Ballroom, the Pershing Lounge (Ahmad Jamal, 1957), and the basement club Budland — first a jazz room featuring Arnett Cobb, Miles Davis, and Billie Holiday — anchoring the 63rd–Cottage Grove nightlife strip.

name: Bud Billiken Club (Chicago Defender youth section)
description: The Defender's youth club/section built around the Bud Billiken character; between 1930 and 1934 approximately 10,000 children's names appeared in the section and were archived at the Carter G. Woodson Regional Library.

name: Checkerboard Lounge
description: South Side blues club long associated with Buddy Guy

name: Club Bagdad
description: South Side jazz club at 840 E. 63rd Street, documented in the Chicago Defender's October 10, 1953 nightlife listings (the 5 Blazes and Terry Timmons).

name: Club DeLisa
description: Famed Bronzeville nightclub whose floor shows starred Black entertainers

name: Cotton Club
description: 1950s Woodlawn jazz club at 6249 S. Cottage Grove Avenue, documented in the October 10, 1953 Chicago Defender (Harold King and Red Allen). A namesake of the Harlem Cotton Club; distinct from both the New York original and the later 1986-2006 South Loop club.

name: Den One
description: Chicago gay club where Ron Hardy began his DJ career in 1974 with two turntables, a mixer, and a reel-to-reel tape deck.

name: El Grotto Supper Club
description: Supper club at 6412 S. Cottage Grove, in Chicago's Pershing Hotel (Woodlawn), operating 1944-1947. Hosted Ivie Anderson, saxophonist George Auld, and singer Ida James; billed as 'Harry Fields' El Grotto Supper Club'; served dinner to the Billikens; fielded a prize-winning float (1946). The Pershing Hotel's Beige Room opened in its space in December 1947. Documented in the University of Chicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide from Chicago Defender citations.
address: 6412 S. Cottage Grove Ave (in the Pershing Hotel)

name: Grand Terrace Cafe
description: Bronzeville nightclub where Earl Hines's orchestra held long residencies
aliases: Grand Terrace Cafe / Grand Terrace Ballroom

name: Green Door Club
description: Englewood, Chicago club documented in a 1959 community-history photograph (photographer unknown) shown in the Living Tracks 'ENT Community Meeting #2' presentation. Its exact street address and operator are unverified in located sources. Not the Green Door Tavern of River North (678 N Orleans St).

name: High Chaparral
description: Clarence Ludd's large South Side soul club at 7740 S. Stony Island Ave., near the northwest corner of 79th and Stony Island; one of the most popular Black clubs of the 1960s and 1970s, hosting local and national icons.
neighborhood: 79th Street commercial corridor (Chatham / Greater Grand Crossing)

name: House of Blues Chicago
description: 1,400-capacity concert hall at 329 N. Dearborn Street in the Marina City complex, opened 1996; a Live Nation venue hosting Buddy Guy's annual January residency and the Sunday World Famous Gospel Brunch.

name: Ida B. Wells Woman's Club
description: Black women's civic club organized by Ida B. Wells in 1893 as the Women's Era Club and later renamed in her honor; first-of-its-kind for African-American women in Chicago. Charter member of the Cook County Women's Clubs; campaigned for the Ida B. Wells housing project (1939).
aliases: Women's Era Club; Ida B. Wells Club

name: International Game Room
description: Calvin Hollis' International Game Room on 47th Street off King Drive, Chicago; the venue where promoter David Risqué gave DJ Celeste Alexander her first DJ gig in the early 1980s.

name: Jazz Showcase
description: Chicago's oldest jazz club (founded 1947 by Joe Segal); 170-seat listening room at 806 S Plymouth Ct (Joe Segal Way), South Loop, in rebuilt Dearborn Station since 2008. Live seven nights a week. Not Black-owned (Segal family); stage, archive, and audience history inseparable from Black artistry.

name: Kingston Mines
description: Lincoln Park blues club at 2548 N. Halsted Street, opened 1968; the oldest continuously operating blues club in Chicago. Grew out of the Kingston Mines Theatre Company (the original Grease premiered there in 1971); two stages; owned by the Pellegrino family.
aliases: Kingston Mines Café; Kingston Mines Company Store

name: Kitty Kat Club
description: Gay nightclub at 611 E. 63rd Street in Woodlawn, a haven for gay South Siders with forward-looking jazz programming (Ahmad Jamal, John Young, King Fleming before their ascents). Two scenes of A Raisin in the Sun (1961) were filmed there.

name: Lee's Unleaded Blues
description: South Side blues club at 7401 S. South Chicago Avenue in Greater Grand Crossing, opened 1983 by Ray and Leola 'Lee' Grey on the site of the 1970s Queen Bee's Lounge; closed 2015, reopened 2024 under Warren Berger.

name: Off The Street Club
description: Off The Street Club is a youth organization in West Garfield Park, Chicago, founded in 1900 — by the organization's own account — and operating continuously into the present. It works as a youth safe-space and development club for West Side youth, offering athletics, tutoring, mentoring, arts programming, and camp. CultureTechLens's institutional research keeps the club for its longevity finding while flagging two cautions: it was founded in 1900, before its neighborhood was Black, and its current governance and funding are unverified in the research record.

name: Pershing Hotel club (Pershing Lounge / Budland)
description: Basement jazz club Budland (later R&B) in the Pershing Hotel at 6400 S. Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Site of Ahmad Jamal's landmark 1958 live recordings. Hosted Arnett Cobb, Miles Davis, and Billie Holiday in its jazz years.
address: 6400 S. Cottage Grove Ave (in the Pershing Hotel)

name: Phyllis Wheatley Club and Home
description: Black women's club and home for young Black women (founded 1896, led by Elizabeth Lindsay Davis); final home at 5128 S. Michigan Ave., Bronzeville; lost to court-ordered demolition after the 2021 endangered listing.

name: Playboy Club (Chicago)
description: Chicago Playboy Club; Hugh Hefner booked Dick Gregory there in 1961, launching his national career.

name: Roberts Show Lounge
description: Herman Roberts's South Side show lounge; starred Nina Simone, Sam Cooke, and Dinah Washington
aliases: Roberts Show Club; Roberts Show Club / Roberts Show Lounge

name: Rosa's Lounge
description: Family-run blues club at 3420 W Armitage Ave, opened 1984 by Italian immigrant Tony Mangiullo and named for his mother Rosa. Opened as a tribute to the South Side blues lounges such as Theresa's Lounge; a community anchor for Chicago blues, still programming live blues as of 2026.

name: Shelter (house club)
description: Chicago underground house/loft-scene nightclub that opened in 1990 and legitimized the city's post-Warehouse party circuit; distinct from New York's Club Shelter.

name: Smart Bar
description: Smartbar opened in July 1982 at 3730 N. Clark under Metro owner Joe Shanahan, with Frankie Knuckles reportedly the first DJ.

name: Stage Lounge
description: Chuck Berry, Art Blakey bookings in the 1950s

name: The Economic Club of Chicago
description: Chicago civic organization. Mellody Hobson became the first African-American woman to head it in 2017.

name: The Rhumboogie
description: Bronzeville nightclub owned by Charlie Glenn; hosted Charlie Parker and T-Bone Walker
aliases: Rhumboogie; 343 East 55th Street; Rhumboogie Cafe; Rhumboogie Café

name: The Warehouse
description: The Warehouse was a DJ-led dance club at 206 S. Jefferson Street in Chicago's West Loop, in a three-story loft building, and is the nightclub widely credited as the birthplace of house music. Promoter Robert Williams opened the club in 1977 and installed New York DJ Frankie Knuckles as resident DJ in March 1977; Knuckles's residency ran to 1982. The room drew a Black, Latino, and largely gay crowd, and CTL's venue research grades it as one of the first clubs where gay and straight, Black, Latinx, and white clubgoers shared a dance floor. The best-supported etymology of "house music" derives the term from this club's name — patrons sought "Warehouse music," and Williams billed events as "house" parties. The City of Chicago landmarked the building, with a period of significance of 1977–1982; after Knuckles's 1982 departure, Williams rebranded the venture as the Music Box with Ron Hardy as resident DJ. CTL's house-music brief is explicit that the club, the DJ practice, and the recorded genre are three separate births, and this record preserves that distinction rather than the lone-inventor myth.
neighborhood: Chicago; Near West Side; West Loop

name: 63rd Street Theatre (Langley Hippodrome)
description: Early 63rd Street vaudeville house

name: Afro-Arts Theater
description: Regional theater at 3900 S. Drexel on Chicago's South Side, opened 1967 by musician/activist Kelan Philip Cohran. A meeting place for Black power activists and, per the Journal of Black Studies, central to the growth of African American consciousness in Chicago, it hosted a weekly cultural extravaganza featuring poets Haki Madhubuti, Carolyn Rodgers, and Useni Eugene Perkins. Gwendolyn Brooks received there on December 28, 1969 what she considered “the most stirring and significant tribute of her life.” Theater as political infrastructure.

name: Auditorium Theatre
description: Roosevelt University; Adler & Sullivan

name: Avalon Regal Theater
description: John Eberson's 1927 Moorish Revival atmospheric theater at 1645 E. 79th St. in South Shore, opened as the Avalon; renamed the New Regal in 1987 by Edward and Bettiann Gardner in honor of the demolished Bronzeville Regal; designated a Chicago Landmark in 1992; purchased by Jerald Gary in 2014 and recommended for a $249,500 Adopt-A-Landmark grant in October 2026.
aliases: Avalon Theater; New Regal Theater; Avalon Regal; The New Regal

name: Black Cinema House
description: Rebuild Foundation site in Chicago hosting film screenings and discussions.

name: Black Ensemble Theater
description: Black theater company at 4450 N. Clark St., Uptown, founded 1976 by Jackie Taylor; mission: eradicate racism through theater arts and community engagement.

name: Chicago Latino Theater Alliance (CLATA)
description: Alliance founded in 2016 by executive director Myrna Salazar with Chicago's three most prominent Latino arts organizations: the National Museum of Mexican Art, the International Latino Cultural Center, and the Puerto Rican Arts Alliance. A nonprofit 501(c)(3), it produces Destinos, the Chicago International Latino Theater Festival, aiming to build the country's leading international Latino theater festival while giving local companies organizational, marketing, and financial support and working toward a permanent home for Chicago's Latino theater artists. The 3rd Destinos (2019) presented 93+ performances; the 5th ran September 14-October 16, 2022, dedicated to Salazar after her death in August 2022.

name: Chicago Theatre
description: State Street movie palace; concerts

name: Cinema/Chicago
description: Cinema/Chicago is the Chicago nonprofit cultural and educational organization that presents the Chicago International Film Festival. Founded in 1964 — its founder, Michael Kutza, served as its chief executive until his retirement at the end of 2018 and remains CEO Emeritus — the organization states its mission as fostering better communication between people of diverse cultures through the art of film and the moving image, and serving Chicago's diverse and under-served audiences with access to world-class cinema. Beyond the October festival, Cinema/Chicago runs year-round programs: the CineYouth Festival each April, showcasing filmmakers 22 and under; the free Summer Screenings series; Community Cinema, bringing free screenings to under-resourced neighborhoods across the city; the Digging Deeper into Movies lecture series with Northwestern University professor Nick Davis; the Chicago Industry Exchange Lab (CIX:Lab), a creative-development program for emerging Illinois filmmakers; and the Black Perspectives program, the festival's year-round showcase for Black American and African-diaspora cinema since 1997. In 2026 the organization was named a Make It Better Foundation Philanthropy Award recipient, and the festival it presents was voted the No. 2 Best Film Festival in the U.S. for 2026 by USA Today readers.

name: Collaboraction Theatre Company
description: Collaboraction Theatre Company (also recorded as Collaboraction) is a Chicago theater company devoted to social-issue-driven contemporary theater. Its documented mainstage work in the evidence corpus is the 2019–20 season, staged at the Kennedy-King College theaters in Englewood — the U Building's 292-seat mainstage and black box theaters at 740 W. 63rd Street. The Kennedy-King College theaters' graph record names that season 'We Are Each Other's Business,' including the fourth annual Peacebook Festival and the 'Red Island' world premiere, and places it as year three of Collaboraction's five-year One City plan. The graph record's era is 2019–2020 and its status Verified, resting on a single BroadwayWorld season announcement; the underlying place research graded the same BroadwayWorld item as press-release-style when auditing the venue record.

name: Congo Square Theatre
description: African American theater company founded in 1999 by Derrick Sanders and Reginald Nelson; one of only two Black Actors' Equity companies in Chicago. Mentored by August Wilson; produced Seven Guitars (2005 Joseph Jefferson Awards sweep) and cultivated Chadwick Boseman (Deep Azure) and Lydia Diamond (Stick Fly).
aliases: Congo Square; Congo Square Theatre Company

description: Logan Square theater; concerts

name: Englewood Theatre
description: Englewood, Chicago movie house: ended burlesque and went movies-only on February 12, 1922 (starting with ‘Hail the Woman’); staged a public wedding on June 28, 1928; modernized in 1949; still advertising films in 1959. Demolition date unresolved in the sources.

name: Ethiopian Art Theatre
description: Short-lived (1922/1923–1925) Chicago-based Black theatre company of the Harlem Renaissance, founded by white director Raymond O'Neil and sponsored by Mrs. Sherwood Anderson; its all-Black performers staged European repertoire (Wilde's Salome, a jazz-accompanied Comedy of Errors) and Black-authored work, including Willis Richardson's The Chip Woman's Fortune — the first Black drama produced on Broadway (Frazee Theatre, May 7, 1923).

name: Kennedy-King College theaters
description: Performing-arts venue at Kennedy-King College, 740 W. 63rd St., Englewood, Chicago: the U Building's state-of-the-art 292-seat mainstage and black box theaters. Collaboraction Theatre Company staged its 2019–20 mainstage season ('We Are Each Other's Business') there — including the fourth annual Peacebook Festival and the 'Red Island' world premiere — as year three of its five-year One City plan. The U Building also houses the Center of Equity for Creative Arts (CECA) and WKKC-FM 89.3.

name: Kimbark Theatre (Kim Theatre)
description: Small early Woodlawn movie house at 6240 S. Kimbark Avenue (between 62nd and 63rd Streets): opened 1913, seated just under 700, closed in the 1960s, later used as a church, vacant for years, demolished January/February 2016.

name: Marquette Theatre
description: 1,200-seat movie house at 3157 W. 63rd Street (Kedzie & 63rd) in Chicago Lawn. Designed by Henry L. Newhouse & F.M. Bernham; opened March 23, 1924; leased for 10 years to Balaban & Katz; operated by the Stern Theater Interests circuit; closed January 4, 1981 with Disney's "The Aristocats"; demolished August 1987; the site became a Walgreens parking lot.

name: Maryland Theatre
description: Maryland Theatre: former movie palace at 855 E. 63rd Street, Chicago (Woodlawn), between S. Drexel and S. Maryland Avenues. Opened in 1928 on the site of the Woodlawn Theatre, seating 1,800. Operated by Balaban & Katz from opening until the 1960s, then part of the ABC Theatres chain. In the 1970s it hosted African-American performing artists. Closed in 1977; vandalized in the 1980s and demolished in the 1990s; the site is now a parking lot. Stood within blocks of the Tivoli Theatre and the Trianon Ballroom.

name: MPAACT (Ma'at Production Association of Afrikan Centered Theatre)
description: Afrikan-centered theater company founded 1990 in Chicago (founding member Shepsu Aakhu): develops new, collaborative Afrikan-centered works through a collective model. Resident playwright Shepsu Aakhu; staged productions at the Greenhouse Theater Center, Lincoln Park (Spoken Word 2020, Swamp Baby 2019, Black and Blue 2018).

name: Original Englewood Theater
description: Turn-of-the-20th-century Englewood movie house at 63rd Street and Normal Boulevard; Lauer Sisters Restaurant later occupied its site. Distinct from the 1926 Englewood Theatre at 63rd & Halsted (CTL-E-1012).

description: Landmark South Side movie palace and stage that headlined the biggest Black entertainers of its day

name: Riviera Theatre
description: Uptown concert hall; opened 1917

description: Ensemble theater company

name: Stratford Theatre
description: Warner Bros. neighborhood theater at 715 W. 63rd St, Englewood. Opened September 4, 1920, with 2,433 seats and a Moller 3-manual 22-rank organ; built for Cooney Brothers National Theaters Corp. Often said to be where Bob Hope got his first start. Torn down.

name: The Second City
description: Chicago improvisational comedy theater. Robert Townsend studied improvisation at its workshop in 1974 as a teenager.

name: Tivoli Theatre
description: Balaban & Katz movie palace at 63rd & Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Opened February 16, 1921; 3,520 seats; Rapp and Rapp, French Baroque. First of the B&K "big three." R&B/jazz showcase in its late years. Closed September 19, 1963; demolished shortly after.

name: Tower Theatre
description: Neighborhood movie house at 1510 E. 63rd St, Woodlawn. Opened early 1926 with just under 3,000 seats; Italian Renaissance by Fridstein & Company for Lubliner & Trinz; acquired by Balaban & Katz in 1928. Closed sometime in the 1950s (exact dates unresolved); later demolished.

name: Uptown Theatre
description: Historic 4,381-seat movie palace at 4816 N. Broadway, Chicago; opened August 18, 1925; designed by Rapp and Rapp for Balaban & Katz; closed to regular audiences since 1981.

name: Basin Street
description: South Side jazz club at 6312 S. Cottage Grove, Chicago (formerly Cadillac Bob's), on the west side of Cottage Grove in the 63rd Street Black nightlife district of Woodlawn. Eddie “Cleanhead” Vinson was part owner (per Chicago Defender, Oct. 23, 1954); the room featured Johnny Griffin, Eddie Vinson, Buddy Smith, Junior Mance, Willie Mabon, Mabel Hunter, Jump Jackson's orchestra, Willie Jones, Betty Dupree, and Phil Thomas in Defender listings (1954–1955). Secondary accounts only.

name: C and C Lounge

A Hammond organ was a house feature (Chicago Daily Defender, Oct 1956); the club's illuminated sign appeared in the opening of the 1980s TV series Crime Stories.

name: Grant Park
description: Downtown Chicago lakefront park (319 acres) that has hosted the Chicago Blues Festival (at the Petrillo Music Shell and festival stages) and the Chicago Gospel Music Festival since the 1980s; the Blues Festival moved to adjacent Millennium Park in 2017.

name: Green Mill Cocktail Lounge
description: Uptown jazz club and cocktail lounge at 4802 N. Broadway, opened in 1907 as Pop Morse's Roadhouse; Prohibition-era speakeasy and Al Capone hangout. Since 1986 it has been the birthplace of the poetry-slam movement (Uptown Poetry Slam).

name: Harold Washington Library Center
description: The Harold Washington Library Center is the main branch of the Chicago Public Library. It is home to YOUmedia, the library's teen digital-learning program, which opened in 2009; Chicago rapper Noname spent time as a teen in the YOUMedia project at the Harold Washington Library. The building houses CPL's Special Collections Division, cited in a finding aid as the holder of the Kuumba collection; a Smithsonian Archives of American Art survey also places the George Cleveland Hall Branch Archives there — 28 linear feet of records dating from 1932 to the 1970s, including remnants of the Special Negro Collection.

name: Harry's Show Lounge
description: 63rd Street show lounge at 432 E. 63rd St. (1947-1963) in Woodlawn; early-career Ramsey Lewis Trio appearances June 6 & 18, 1956 (with George 'Stardust' Greene and Eldee Young); also the Johnny Pate trio (1955), Les Tucker Trio (1958), and the Rhythm Aces (1958).

name: Lincoln Gardens
description: Nightclub and dance hall at 459 East 31st Street (South Cottage Grove), the largest dance hall on Chicago's South Side until the Savoy Ballroom opened in 1927. Reinvented in 1918 by Black entrepreneurs Virgil Williams and William Bottoms; renamed Lincoln Gardens in 1921. Resident home of King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band (1922–1924), where Louis Armstrong came north to play second cornet. Closed June 1927 after a bombing.
aliases: Royal Gardens; Royal Gardens Café; New Charleston Café; Café de Paris

name: Muzic Box (Music Box)
description: House music club at 326 North Michigan Avenue (1983–1988) with resident DJ Ron Hardy. The raw, high-energy counterpart to the Warehouse — the room where acid house broke: Hardy premiered Phuture's "Acid Tracks" there, and his reel-to-reel edits and fearless programming defined a harder Chicago sound. Closed in 1987.

description: 75th Street jazz lounge where tenor saxophonist Von Freeman held court on Tuesday nights

name: Reggies
description: South Loop rock club

name: Robert Hall (clothing) / later Taste disco
description: Former Robert Hall Clothes store at 6331 S. Lowe in Englewood (1950s-60s); the building later became the Taste Disco Lounge.
aliases: Robert Hall Clothes (Englewood); Taste Disco Lounge; Taste

name: Savoy Ballroom
description: The Savoy Ballroom was a Bronzeville dance hall at 4733 S. Parkway (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), at 47th Street, celebrated in the graph record as the "World's Finest Ballroom" for Black dancers. It opened in November 1927 as part of a single commercial complex with the Regal Theater and the South Center Department Store, developed by a syndicate headed by Harry M. and Louis Englestein and operated by dance promoter I. Jay Faggen; the complex helped make 47th Street's reputation as the "Harlem of Chicago." The ballroom accommodated more than 4,000 people and anchored the 47th and South Parkway bright-light district. University of Chicago exhibit research treats it as a major jazz center, and CTL's corridor research dates its era from the late 1920s to its closing in 1954, with demolition in the early 1970s; the site is now occupied by the Harold Washington Cultural Center. Corpus sources dispute the exact end dates, and this record flags that dispute rather than smoothing it.

name: Schorling's Park
description: Schorling's Park was a Chicago ballpark on 39th Street between Princeton and Wentworth Streets, at 39th and Wentworth, whose life the Society for American Baseball Research divides into a white major-league act, a Black baseball act, and a final decline. Opened as South Side Park, it hosted its first game on April 21, 1900, as the original Chicago home of Charles Comiskey's White Stockings, later the White Sox. After Comiskey moved his club north, tavern owner John Schorling leased the grounds, rebuilt the stands Comiskey had removed, and in 1911 entered partnership with Rube Foster. The Chicago American Giants played their first game there on May 13, 1911, and the park became Black baseball's Chicago home: Foster's club won Negro National League pennants in 1920, 1921, and 1922 and Negro World Series titles in 1926 and 1927 on that ground. SABR records crowds, a 1919 riot-era National Guard encampment, night baseball in 1930, and years of mixed sporting and civic use. Vandals set fire to the wooden park on December 23, 1940; it was never rebuilt, the American Giants moved to Comiskey Park for 1941 onward, and Wentworth Gardens housing was later built on the site.
aliases: Schorling Park; South Side Park; White Sox Park; 39th Street Grounds; Cole's Park; American Giants Park; Cole's American Giants Park

Theatre Co. founded by actress/director Karla Galvan; theater house and school at 3117 W 63rd St serving Marquette Park and surrounding communities with affordable performing-arts classes; presenter in the Destinos Chicago International Latino Theater Festival.

name: The Forum (Bronzeville)
description: The Forum at 318 E 43rd Street in Bronzeville, Chicago: an 1897 building that was once an entertainment venue for Chicago's Black artists and musicians; under redevelopment since 2021 (led by Bernard Loyd of Urban Juncture) to return it to a performance venue with banquet hall, retail, and restaurant space.

name: The Power Plant
description: The Power Plant was a house-music club at 1015 N. Halsted Street, on Goose Island, founded by Frankie Knuckles in 1983 after he left the Warehouse. The City of Chicago's Warehouse landmark report — one of this record's own sources — verifies the address and the founding: when the Warehouse doubled admission in late 1982 and grew more commercial, Knuckles left and established his own club, and his followers came with him. Knuckles DJed at the Power Plant until 1986, when he returned to New York City and established Def Mix with David Morales. Where the Warehouse had been a largely gay, Black and Latino room, scene accounts describe Knuckles translating the sound to a broader audience at the Power Plant — a characterization CTL's research carries as Provisional, from a single archivist source, and this record keeps that grade visible. The building's fate after Knuckles's 1986 departure is unresolved in CTL's venue research, so this record makes no claim about the site's current status.

name: White City Ballroom
description: The White City Ballroom was the ballroom of the White City Amusement Park at 63rd Street and South Park Avenue (now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), on the Woodlawn / Greater Grand Crossing edge of the South Side. The park opened on May 26, 1905 (one Illinois history source gives May 27 — a minor contradiction the corpus notes), spread over fourteen acres, and rivaled Coney Island; its ballroom was built for 1,000 dancers, alongside the College Inn restaurant seating 2,500. The graph record describes it as a big-band ballroom within White City, and the University of Chicago's jazz guide — the record's source — documents the ballroom in Chicago Defender citations, including a Wolfscale's Band appearance on June 22, 1918 and a White City advertisement on July 2, 1921, with the room operating into the 1920s–1940s. The park fell into financial distress and bankruptcy in 1933–34 and most of it closed in 1934; its roller rink survived, renamed Park City Roller Rink, until 1958, and the site was later occupied by Parkway Gardens. Tier is R: support rests on one guide source plus CTL's establishment findings.
address: 63rd St & S. Parkway Blvd (now MLK Jr. Dr.)
